title: Where Will Palantir Stock Be in 1 Year?
detail:
Where Will Palantir Stock Be in 1 Year?
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 2:59 PM MST 4 min read
PLTR
NVDA
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase

The artificial intelligence (AI) play still looks intact even as Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock plunges. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 is up 11% year to date, and the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), which is heavily weighted toward AI right now, is up 11%. Both of these gains are impressive, considering that Nvidia stock, which is a major component of the index, is down more than 12%.

However, Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) is also down. It's lost 5% this year despite fantastic operating results, and it's still wildly expensive. Where could it be in one year?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Sovereign AI for enterprises

Palantir has been the poster child for AI stocks for years. Its groundbreaking AI platform helps companies analyze data to detect patterns and make decisions while keeping their information private.

What began as a program for the military and U.S. intelligence, including seed money from the CIA, has bloomed into a broad business serving all sectors. The company's AI platform (AIP), which is geared toward commercial organizations, is thriving, driving incredible growth for the whole company.

In the third quarter, total revenue increased 96% from the year-ago period, and U.S. commercial revenue was up 148%.

However, as AI continues to develop and handle more daily tasks, competition is creeping in, both from AI agents and competitors specifically in this space, like Databricks and Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW).

Palantir claims that its edge lies in its sovereignty, meaning clients keep their data private and proprietary. The results show that clients agree. They're seeing excellent results from the partnership, which is the main reason they're likely to stay, at least in the near term.

What could happen in a year?

Palantir stock is dropping for two distinct reasons even though it's growing like wildfire. One is the threat of competition as AI flourishes, and the other is the stock's premium price tag. It trades at 118 times trailing 12-month earnings and 59 times trailing 12-month sales, and it's the most expensive stock in the S&P 500 on a price-to-sales basis.

With that kind of price, there's little room for error or negative market sentiment for any reason.

In the third quarter, for example, U.S. commercial revenue growth dropped down the tiniest of notches from 149% last quarter, and total contract value increased 6%, down from 49%. These things matter when the valuation is as high as Palantir's.

Is Palantir Overvalued, or Is It Still a Buy at This Price?
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) has attracted considerable attention among businesses and investors alike in recent years. Its data analytics tools have driven eye-popping productivity gains for its clients. As such, interest in its products has soared, and annual revenue growth is approaching triple-digit percentages.

Unfortunately, this has also drawn attention to its valuation, as rapid revenue growth typically means a stock will trade at a considerable premium. Despite its impressive revenue growth, I believe Palantir stock is overvalued. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Why Palantir has grown so rapidly

Palantir began as a company focused on supporting national defense and intelligence agencies. Its tools employ artificial intelligence to analyze data and deliver insights. In its early days, the help it provided to U.S. intelligence services in finding Osama bin Laden gained the company considerable attention.

However, seeing the limits of growth within that field, it turned its expertise to the commercial sector. While that broadening of its customer base led to increased growth, it was the release of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) that was the game changer.

Palantir began offering potential customers the opportunity to enroll in "boot camps" where they were able to immediately see how AIP could be applied to their actual business problems, and as a result, many of its clients began to discover ways to use it to noticeably increase productivity.

Among these companies is GE Aerospace, which applied AIP to fleet management and supply chain coordination, thereby increasing engine production. AIP also helped AIG automate insurance underwriting for more complicated commercial lines of business.

Such improvements helped drive Palantir's revenue to nearly $5.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 92% from the prior-year period, with a blowout Q3 boosting that growth.

Moreover, since its costs and expenses grew more slowly than revenue, its net income was nearly $3.1 billion during the same period. That was a 201% year-over-year increase. Amid this performance, it is not too surprising that Palantir stock is up by more than 2,300% since the beginning of 2023.

For 2026, revenue will grow 91% if the company's forecasts hold. However, analysts predict that growth will slow to 53% in 2027.

A close-up of a General Motors corporate sign by lindaparton via Adobe Stock

For more than a century, legacy automaker General Motors (GM) called the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) home. As of Nov. 17, 2026, that era is over. The Detroit automaker is officially moving its primary listing to Nasdaq, with its existing ticker symbol, GM, staying the same. The NYSE relationship dates back to 1911, and GM returned to the exchange after its 2010 bankruptcy. Still, the move isn't as surprising as it might seem.

A growing number of companies are aligning themselves with the tech-heavy exchange, chasing proximity to tech stocks as investors rush to back the AI buildout. Walmart (WMT), Hilton (HLT), and Palantir (PLTR) are among the names that have recently made the shift. GM, however, adds a first of its own. It is set to become the first legacy automaker on the Nasdaq. Finance chief Paul Jacobson said that GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for its stockholders, which makes Nasdaq a natural home for the listing as the company grows.

The backdrop makes the timing even more interesting.

Legacy automakers, squeezed by higher costs, have been trying their hand at cheaper, software-heavy vehicles to keep up with Chinese rivals, and a Nasdaq listing helps GM present itself as a technology company as much as a carmaker.
